title: Mosaics in Space vs. Bubbles in Space-Time: Random First-Order Transition vs. Dynamic Facilitation in the Glass Transition — Fourteen orders of magnitude in viscosity with near-zero structural change; Kauzmann's 1948 configurational entropy crisis & Kirkpatrick-Thirumalai-Wolynes entropic mosaics; Berthier & Ninarello's Swap Monte Carlo revolution, 2D zero-temperature glass transition & Biroli-Bouchaud-Ladieu's fifth-order dielectric amorphous order; Chandler & Garrahan's kinetically constrained space-time bubbles & Scalliet-Guiselin-Berthier's 30-ms facilitation cascades; VFT vs. parabolic activation math, point-to-set cavity power & spotting glass-transition tests in disguise

teenKit.tldr: When you cool certain liquids past their freezing point, they turn into glass without forming crystals, causing their thickness (viscosity) to explode by fourteen orders of magnitude while looking totally unchanged under a microscope.
teenKit.whyItMatters: This strange transformation explains everything from how window glass ages and how cell biology works to how pharmaceutical drugs stay stable over time without crystallizing.
keyTakeaways: The glass transition is considered one of the deepest unsolved problems in modern solid-state physics because structural snapshots look identical while the material's internal movement slows down to a near-complete stop.
The Random First-Order Transition (RFOT) theory argues that liquids form growing internal 'mosaics' of order that trap molecules as things get colder.
The rival Dynamic Facilitation theory claims that glassiness isn't about static structure at all, but rather space-time bubbles where movement cascades through local pockets.

vocab.meaning: A fluid's natural resistance to flow, which measures how thick or sluggishly sticky a liquid behaves.
A liquid that has been cooled safely past its normal freezing point without actually crystallizing into a solid.
A mathematical count of how many different internal arrangements or configurations a bunch of molecules can take.
The kinetic theory that molecules in a glass only move when a neighboring space opens up, creating cascading chains of motion through space and time.

quiz.question: What happens to the viscosity of a supercooled liquid near the glass transition temperature?
options: It stays completely flat and steady
It explodes by about fourteen orders of magnitude
It turns into a gas instantly
quiz.explanation: Viscosity skyrockets by fourteen orders of magnitude, turning flowing liquid into rigid glass within a tiny temperature window.

quiz.question: What is Walter Kauzmann's 1948 paradox about?
options: The infinite speed of light in glass
An impending crisis where extrapolated configurational entropy hits zero
The unexpected magnetic properties of hot liquids
Why water expands when it freezes
quiz.explanation: Kauzmann pointed out that if you extrapolate downward, a liquid's internal disorder choices would drop to zero, creating a thermodynamic crisis.

quiz.question: How do proponents of Dynamic Facilitation view the glass transition?
options: As a purely thermodynamic crisis controlled by static mosaic size
As a kinetic traffic jam where movement depends entirely on local space-time bubbles
As an optical illusion caused by light refraction
quiz.explanation: Dynamic Facilitation treats glassiness as a kinetic puzzle of trajectory space-time bubbles where molecules move only when triggered by local neighbors.
